items.q: In the pathoanatomy of hallux valgus, lateral drift of the hallux and medial drift of the first metatarsal head lead to altered muscle mechanics. Which muscle plantarly migrates, losing its abduction power and acting as a flexor and pronator of the hallux?
items.e: As hallux valgus progresses, the abductor hallucis muscle migrates plantarly relative to the metatarsal head, losing its lateral-to-medial abduction pull and instead acting as a flexor and pronator (evertor) of the hallux.
items.note: Accurate pathoanatomical concept directly aligned with gold-standard orthopaedic literature.

items.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with symptomatic hallux valgus. Radiographs demonstrate an increased distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA) with parallel articular surfaces across the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, confirming a congruent deformity. Which principle governs surgical decision-making in this patient?
o: Soft-tissue release alone is contraindicated because it creates an incongruent joint
Isolated distal soft-tissue release reliably restores normal alignment in congruent deformities
A simple bunionectomy (Silver procedure) is sufficient when the MTP joint is congruent
Excision of the base of the proximal phalanx (Keller procedure) is the first-line treatment
items.e: In a congruent hallux valgus deformity, correcting the alignment by distal soft-tissue release alone creates an incongruent joint. A DMAA-correcting osteotomy (such as a biplanar chevron) or extra-articular osteotomies are required.
items.note: Standard surgical principle for juvenile/congruent hallux valgus accurately represented.

items.q: A 48-year-old runner presents with pain and stiffness of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint during push-off. Physical examination demonstrates preserved motion with pain only at the extremes of dorsiflexion, and no pain during mid-range motion (negative grind test). Radiographs reveal mild joint space narrowing and a prominent dorsal metatarsal osteophyte (Coughlin and Shurnas Grade 1/2 hallux rigidus). What is the operative procedure of choice?
items.e: Cheilectomy (excision of the dorsal osteophyte and upper 25-30% of the metatarsal head) is indicated for Grade 1 and 2 hallux rigidus with pain restricted to extreme dorsiflexion. First MTP joint arthrodesis is reserved for advanced stage 3 and 4 disease with mid-range pain.
items.note: Clear indication matching standard guidelines for Coughlin and Shurnas grading.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman complains of burning pain in her forefoot that radiates into her third and fourth toes, described as 'walking on a pebble'. Mediolateral compression of the metatarsal heads combined with direct pressure over the third web space produces a palpable click and pain. What is the name of this sign, and where is the lesion located relative to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament?
o: Sullivan sign; proximal to the ligament
Mulder click; distal to the ligament
Lachman test; proximal to the ligament
Silfverskiöld test; distal to the ligament
items.e: A Mulder click is elicited by squeezing the forefoot mediolaterally while pressing the affected intermetatarsal web space, representing a Morton neuroma (perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve located distal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament).
items.note: Factually flawless, testing physical sign and anatomical relation of Morton neuroma.

items.q: A patient with bilateral cavus foot deformity from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease presents with severe lesser toe deformities. Clinical examination reveals hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, and flexion at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Which deformity is described?
items.e: A claw toe is characterised by MTP joint hyperextension, PIP joint flexion, and DIP joint flexion. It is usually bilateral, affects multiple toes, and is commonly caused by intrinsic weakness in neuromuscular disorders or cavus feet.
items.note: Classic distinction between lesser toe deformities (hammer vs mallet vs claw).

items.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with lateral forefoot pain over the fifth metatarsal head. Radiographs reveal an increased 4-5 intermetatarsal angle (>10°). According to Coughlin's classification of bunionette (tailor's bunion) deformities, which type does this represent and what operative management is indicated?
o: Type III; diaphyseal oblique or proximal osteotomy
items.e: Coughlin Type III bunionette deformity is defined by an increased 4-5 intermetatarsal angle (>8-10°). Treatment requires a diaphyseal oblique or proximal osteotomy to narrow the 4-5 intermetatarsal angle.
items.note: Accurate presentation of Coughlin bunionette classification and treatment principles.

items.q: During a Scarf osteotomy (Z-shaped diaphyseal osteotomy) for moderate hallux valgus, failure of technical execution leads to telescoping of the diaphyseal cortical bone fragments into one another. Which complication directly results from this structural compromise?
o: Hallux varus due to overcorrection of the intermetatarsal angle
Troughing resulting in metatarsal head elevation and loss of height
Avascular necrosis due to injury to the first dorsal metatarsal artery
items.e: Troughing occurs during a Scarf osteotomy when the cortical fragments telescope into the softer cancellous bone of the metatarsal shaft. This results in loss of height and elevation of the metatarsal head (elevatus), leading to transfer metatarsalgia.
items.note: High-yield surgical complication question with clear anatomical/technical correlation.

items.q: An American football player sustains a severe hyperdorsiflexion injury to the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint on artificial turf. Examination shows marked vertical instability (positive MTP Lachman test), and plain radiographs confirm proximal migration of the sesamoids with sesamoid diastasis (Grade III turf toe). What is the appropriate definitive management?
o: Nonsurgical management with a metatarsal pad and boot immobilisation
Surgical repair of the plantar plate complex
items.e: Grade III turf toe involves a complete rupture of the plantar capsuloligamentous complex (plantar plate), causing sesamoid diastasis, proximal sesamoid displacement, and vertical MTP instability (positive Lachman test). Grade III injuries require surgical repair of the plantar plate.
items.note: Correct treatment indication for high-grade athletic forefoot trauma.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with medial ankle pain and flattening of the medial longitudinal arch. Clinical examination demonstrates forefoot abduction ('too many toes' sign from behind). Which physical examination maneuver is the most sensitive test for detecting tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction?
items.e: The single-limb heel rise test is the most sensitive physical examination test for tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction. Patients are either unable to perform a single-limb heel rise or fail to demonstrate normal inversion of the hindfoot on heel rise.
items.note: Accurate, standard question directly testing the most sensitive physical exam finding for tibialis posterior dysfunction.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman presents with progressive medial ankle pain and flatfoot deformity. Weight-bearing radiographs show a Meary angle of 20 degrees convex plantar and 45% talonavicular uncoverage. On clinical examination, the hindfoot valgus is completely flexible. Which operative procedure combination is most appropriate?
o: Isolated tenosynovectomy of the tibialis posterior tendon
Flexor digitorum longus transfer to the navicular with medializing calcaneal osteotomy and lateral column lengthening
items.e: This patient has Stage IIB adult acquired flatfoot / progressive collapsing foot deformity (flexible flatfoot with forefoot abduction and >30-40% talonavicular uncoverage). Joint-sparing reconstruction combining flexor digitorum longus (FDL) transfer to the navicular, medializing displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO), and lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy) is the treatment of choice.
items.note: Correctly tests the surgical management algorithm for Johnson & Strom Stage IIB / PCFD flexible flatfoot with significant abduction.

items.q: A 48-year-old patient undergoes an Evans lateral column lengthening osteotomy as part of a joint-sparing reconstruction for a flexible flatfoot deformity. Which of the following is the most common complication specifically associated with lateral column lengthening?
o: Lateral column overload and lateral foot pain
Tarsal tunnel syndrome from tibial nerve traction
Deltoid ligament rupture causing severe ankle valgus
items.e: Lateral column overload resulting in lateral foot pain is the most common complication of lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy or calcaneocuboid distraction arthrodesis).
items.note: Standard board-style question on specific complications of flatfoot osteotomies.

items.q: In Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (HMSN type I), muscle imbalance leads to progressive pes cavus deformity. Which specific pair of antagonist muscles becomes unbalanced to cause the characteristic plantarflexed first ray (forefoot pronation)?
o: Weak tibialis posterior versus strong peroneus brevis
Weak tibialis anterior versus strong peroneus longus
Weak peroneus longus versus strong tibialis anterior
Weak flexor hallucis longus versus strong extensor hallucis longus
items.e: In Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, muscle weakness selectively affects the tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis early on. The weak tibialis anterior paired against a strong peroneus longus causes a plantarflexed first ray (forefoot pronation/valgus).
items.note: Directly tests classic muscle imbalance pathomechanics in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
items.reason: repeats cai20261115_089 / b566 (CMT plantarflexed first ray)

items.q: A 22-year-old man presents with high-arched feet, lateral foot pain, and recurrent ankle sprains. Examination reveals hindfoot varus. During the Coleman block test, placing a block under the lateral heel and lateral forefoot allows the first ray to drop off, resulting in complete correction of the hindfoot varus to neutral. What does this result indicate regarding surgical management?
o: The deformity is hindfoot-driven, requiring a lateral calcaneal osteotomy or arthrodesis
The deformity is forefoot-driven, requiring a first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy and plantar fascia release
The deformity is rigid, necessitating a triple arthrodesis
The ankle is unstable, requiring an isolated Broström reconstruction without bony procedures
items.e: Correction of hindfoot varus during the Coleman block test indicates a flexible, forefoot-driven cavus deformity caused by a plantarflexed first ray. Management should target the forefoot with a dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal base, plantar fascia release, and tendon rebalancing.
items.note: High-yield interpretation of the Coleman block test for cavus foot surgical planning.

items.q: In triple arthrodesis performed for severe rigid foot deformities, which joint is considered the key joint because its fusion eliminates virtually all hindfoot motion, and is also the most common site of non-union?
items.e: The talonavicular joint is the key joint in a triple arthrodesis. Fusion of the talonavicular joint alone eliminates almost all motion across the hindfoot complex. Additionally, non-union is most commonly encountered at the talonavicular joint.
items.note: Factually accurate and classic entrance exam question on triple arthrodesis mechanics.

items.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with a progressive, painful unilateral pes cavus deformity of the right foot. The contralateral left foot is completely normal on clinical and radiographic examination. Which investigation is most essential as the next step in evaluation?
o: Genetic testing for PMP22 gene duplication
Nerve conduction studies of the lower limbs only
items.e: Unilateral pes cavus is considered to be caused by a spinal cord lesion (such as tethered cord, syringomyelia, or spinal dysraphism) until proven otherwise, necessitating an MRI of the whole spine.
items.note: Red-flag evaluation rule for unilateral pes cavus in young patients.

items.q: A 40-year-old runner presents with persistent medial heel pain refractory to standard conservative treatment for plantar fasciitis. MRI of the foot reveals selective fatty degeneration and atrophy of the abductor digiti minimi muscle. Entrapment of which nerve accounts for these clinical and MRI findings?
o: First branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter nerve)
items.e: Entrapment of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter nerve or inferior calcaneal nerve) causes chronic medial heel pain mimicking plantar fasciitis. Selective atrophy of the abductor digiti minimi muscle on MRI is characteristic of Baxter nerve entrapment.
items.note: Classic neurovascular entrapment syndrome question testing Baxter nerve anatomy and MRI signs.

items.q: A 42-year-old recreational athlete presents with posterior calf pain after feeling a sudden pop during a tennis match. On physical examination with the patient prone and knees flexed to 90 degrees, the injured foot is observed to hang in neutral/dorsiflexion compared to the resting plantarflexion of the uninjured foot. Which named clinical sign is demonstrated?
items.e: The Matles test assesses the loss of resting plantarflexion tension in an acutely ruptured Achilles tendon; with the knees flexed to 90 degrees in a prone position, the injured foot hangs in neutral or dorsiflexion compared to the normal resting equinus of the contralateral side.
items.note: Accurate, well-formatted question directly testing a classic clinical exam sign for acute Achilles rupture.

items.q: A 24-year-old ballet dancer presents with severe posterior ankle pain aggravated by forced plantarflexion. Posterior ankle arthroscopy is planned for excision of a symptomatic os trigonum. To avoid injuring the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle, which anatomic landmark must be identified so the surgeon stays lateral to it?
items.e: During posterior ankle arthroscopy using posterolateral and posteromedial portals in the prone position, the flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendon serves as the crucial landmark. The surgeon must remain lateral to the FHL to protect the medial-lying tibial neurovascular bundle.
items.note: High-yield surgical landmark question directly supported by Campbell's orthopaedic principles.

items.q: According to the Eckert-Davis classification for superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR) injuries in acute peroneal tendon dislocation, an elevation of the fibrocartilaginous fibular rim along with the SPR is categorized as:
items.e: Eckert-Davis Grade 2 involves elevation of the fibrocartilaginous fibular rim together with the superior peroneal retinaculum. Grade 1 is SPR stripped with periosteum, Grade 3 is a bony avulsion ('fleck sign'), and Grade 4 is SPR torn from its calcaneal attachment.
items.note: Clear classification question testing standard superspeciality depth.

items.q: A 38-year-old runner with a cavovarus foot deformity undergoes surgery for chronic lateral ankle pain. Exploration reveals a longitudinal split tear of the peroneus brevis tendon involving approximately 35% of its cross-sectional area. What is the standard management for this tendon tear?
o: Tenodesis of peroneus brevis to peroneus longus
Debridement and tubularisation of the peroneus brevis
Complete excision of peroneus brevis without repair
Flexor hallucis longus transfer to fifth metatarsal
items.e: For longitudinal split tears of the peroneus brevis involving less than 50% of the cross-sectional area, debridement and tubularisation are recommended. If more than 50% of the tendon is involved, tenodesis to the peroneus longus is indicated.
items.note: Standard management threshold question frequently assessed in foot and ankle subspecialty exams.

items.q: A 46-year-old runner presents with chronic insertional Achilles tendinopathy and posterosuperior heel pain. Radiographs demonstrate a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity. Which radiographic angle measurement is characteristic of a Haglund deformity?
items.e: A Fowler-Philip angle greater than 75 degrees on a lateral foot radiograph indicates a posterosuperior calcaneal prominence characteristic of a Haglund deformity (often associated with Haglund syndrome).
items.note: Classic radiographic criterion question for Haglund syndrome.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with a neglected Achilles tendon rupture sustained 6 weeks ago. Intraoperative exploration after debridement of fibrous scar tissue reveals a tendon gap of 4 cm. According to the Kuwada classification, what is the stage and recommended surgical management?
o: Stage III; V-Y advancement or gastrocnemius recession
Stage IV; FHL tendon transfer combined with tendon graft
items.e: Kuwada Stage III describes a complete chronic rupture with a gap of 3 to 6 cm after debridement. Recommended management includes V-Y aponeurotic advancement, gastrocnemius recession, or tendon grafting (Stage II is <3 cm, Stage IV is >6 cm).
items.note: Standard surgical classification and management question.

items.q: Anterior ankle arthroscopy is performed for symptomatic anterior bony ankle impingement. When establishing the standard anterolateral portal just lateral to the peroneus tertius, which nerve structure is at the greatest risk of injury?
o: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve
items.e: The intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve is at highest risk when establishing the anterolateral portal (lateral to peroneus tertius), representing the most common nerve complication in ankle arthroscopy.
items.note: High-yield surgical complication question based on standard arthroscopic portals.

items.q: A 54-year-old diabetic male presents with a warm, red, and swollen right foot following a minor twist. On examination, the foot surface temperature is 3 °C higher than the contralateral foot. When the limb is elevated for one minute, the erythema resolves completely. Plain weight-bearing radiographs of the foot are entirely normal. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
o: Immobilisation and non-weight bearing in a total contact cast (TCC)
Urgent open realignment and internal fixation of the tarsometatarsal joints
Empiric oral antibiotics for cellulitis and encouragement of full weight-bearing
Immediate fitting with a custom Charcot restraint orthotic walker (CROW)
items.e: The positive Brodsky elevation test (erythema resolving within 1 minute of elevation) differentiates Charcot neuroarthropathy from cellulitis. A warm, swollen neuropathic foot with normal radiographs represents Eichenholtz Stage 0 (Shibata prodromal stage), which requires immediate immobilisation and offloading in a total contact cast (TCC) to prevent bone collapse.
items.note: Accurate clinical presentation and evidence-based initial management for Eichenholtz Stage 0 Charcot.

items.q: A 62-year-old diabetic patient with peripheral arterial disease and a non-healing plantar forefoot ulcer is being evaluated for microvascular healing potential. Which of the following non-invasive vascular measurement thresholds is considered the minimum level associated with predictable wound healing?
items.e: Minimum requirements for diabetic foot wound healing include a toe pressure greater than 40 mmHg (normal >70 mmHg), TcPO2 greater than 30-40 mmHg, and ABI greater than 0.45. An ABI >1.3 indicates non-compressible calcified vessels (Mönckeberg sclerosis), making toe pressure and TcPO2 more reliable indicators.
items.note: Factually correct cutoff values per Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics.

items.q: According to the Meggitt-Wagner classification system for diabetic foot ulcers, a deep ulcer extending down to the joint capsule or bone that is complicated by an associated deep tissue abscess or osteomyelitis is classified as:
items.e: Under the Meggitt-Wagner classification: Grade 0 is intact skin; Grade 1 is a superficial ulcer; Grade 2 is a deep ulcer to tendon, capsule, or bone without abscess or osteomyelitis; Grade 3 is a deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis, or septic arthritis; Grade 4 is forefoot gangrene; and Grade 5 is whole-foot gangrene.
items.note: Standard classification question with unambiguous single correct answer.

items.q: Which anatomical region (Brodsky classification) is most commonly involved in Charcot neuroarthropathy (~60-70% of cases) and typically results in a rocker-bottom foot deformity with high risk of plantar ulceration?
o: Type 2: Hindfoot (subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid joints)
items.e: Brodsky Type 1 involves the midfoot (tarsometatarsal Lisfranc and naviculocuneiform joints) and accounts for 60-70% of Charcot cases, commonly causing tarsal collapse and a rocker-bottom foot deformity with plantar ulceration over bony prominences. Type 3A involves the ankle joint and carries the worst overall prognosis.
items.note: Classic exam topic and distribution data verified against standards.

items.q: Percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening is performed in neuropathic diabetic patients with recalcitrant plantar forefoot ulcers to reduce peak forefoot pressures. What is the most common specific complication associated with overlengthening during this procedure?
o: Transfer plantar ulceration to the heel
items.e: Achilles tendon lengthening reduces peak forefoot pressures and lowers forefoot ulcer recurrence by approximately 75% at 2 years. However, overlengthening results in a calcaneus deformity, shifting peak plantar loading and causing transfer ulceration to the heel.
items.note: High-yield surgical complication question direct from Campbell's.

items.q: A 58-year-old neuropathic diabetic patient presents with a deep, foul-smelling ulcer over the first metatarsal head. On clinical examination, a sterile metal probe easily touches bone at the base of the wound. Which of the following is considered the absolute GOLD STANDARD diagnostic test to confirm osteomyelitis?
o: Bone biopsy for histology and deep culture
items.e: Bone biopsy (obtained percutaneously through uninfected skin or intraoperatively) sent for histology and microbiologic culture is the gold standard for confirming diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Superficial swabs are unreliable as they reflect skin colonisers rather than deep pathogens.
items.note: Clear gold-standard question frequently tested in SS exams.

items.q: Sammarco described four core principles of 'superconstruct' fixation for complex realignment arthrodesis in unstable Charcot foot deformities. Which of the following statements represents a violation of these superconstruct principles?
o: Extending fusion beyond the zone of injury to include unaffected adjacent joints
Performing bony resection to shorten the foot and decompress surrounding soft tissues
Applying internal fixation hardware exclusively on the dorsal (compression) side of the midfoot
Utilising the strongest internal fixation hardware tolerated by the soft-tissue envelope
items.e: Superconstruct principles require applying fixation devices in the position of maximum mechanical advantage, specifically on the plantar (tension) side of the foot (e.g., plantar plating or axial beams), not on the dorsal side. The four principles are: extend fusion beyond injury zone, shorten bone to decompress soft tissues, use strongest hardware tolerated, and place hardware in maximum mechanical advantage positions.
items.note: Accurate assessment of Sammarco's superconstruct principles.

items.q: During a transtibial (below-knee) amputation for non-reconstructable diabetic foot infection, which technical parameter is correctly advocated to ensure ideal prosthetic fit and optimal function?
o: The fibula should be transected 1 to 2 cm shorter than the tibia
The ideal tibial bone length is 20 to 25 cm below the joint line
An equal anterior-posterior skin flap design is superior to a long posterior myocutaneous flap
Transtibial amputation increases metabolic energy expenditure by 60–100% over normal walking
items.e: In a transtibial amputation, the fibula is cut 1–2 cm shorter than the tibia to prevent distal lateral skin breakdown. Ideal tibial length is 12–15 cm (not 20–25 cm) below the joint line. A long posterior flap (Burgess) is standard, and energy cost increases by 10–40% (60–100% is seen in above-knee amputations).
items.note: The original draft had option A as the correct fact but incorrectly marked option B (which stated an erroneous length of 20-25 cm). Fixed key index to 0.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete undergoes a modified Broström-Gould procedure (lateral ligament imbrication reinforced with the inferior extensor retinaculum) for chronic mechanical lateral ankle instability. Postoperatively, the patient reports localized numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most susceptible to iatrogenic injury during this specific surgical approach?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve is the most common nerve injured during surgical procedures for chronic lateral ankle instability, including the modified Broström-Gould repair. Sural nerve injury can also occur, but it is less frequent.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question directly supported by Campbell's and exam notes.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon is performing an ankle arthrodesis for end-stage post-traumatic ankle osteoarthritis. To achieve optimal functional gait and avoid postoperative genu recurvatum or lateral foot overload, in which alignment should the talocrural joint be fused?
o: 5° plantarflexion, 5° hindfoot varus, neutral rotation, and slight anterior talar translation
5° dorsiflexion, neutral hindfoot alignment, 15° internal rotation, and slight posterior talar translation
Neutral dorsiflexion, 5° hindfoot varus, 5-10° external rotation, and slight anterior talar translation
Neutral dorsiflexion, 5° hindfoot valgus, 5-10° external rotation, and slight posterior talar translation
items.e: The ideal position for ankle arthrodesis is neutral dorsiflexion (90°), 5° hindfoot valgus, external rotation equal to the contralateral side (5-10°), and slight posterior translation of the talus. Placing the joint in equinus leads to knee hyperextension (genu recurvatum), whereas varus alignment causes lateral foot overload.
items.note: Standard high-yield orthopaedic board question with precise position parameters.

items.q: A 24-year-old rugby player sustains an ankle injury involving external rotation and dorsiflexion during a tackle. On physical examination, pain is elicited in the syndesmotic region upon passive external rotation of the foot while the knee is flexed at 90°. Which of the following statements regarding high ankle (syndesmotic) sprains is CORRECT based on anatomical and diagnostic criteria?
o: The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL) is the first ligament to fail during an external rotation-dorsiflexion mechanism.
The external rotation stress test (Kleiger test) is the most sensitive clinical examination test for syndesmotic sprains.
A tibiofibular clear space measured 1 cm above the plafond on an AP radiograph is considered normal if it exceeds 6 mm.
The Hopkin squeeze test is the diagnostic gold standard for confirming syndesmotic diastasis of over 2 mm.
items.e: The external rotation stress test (Kleiger test) is the most sensitive clinical physical examination test for syndesmotic sprains. The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL) is the first structure to fail, a tibiofibular clear space over 6 mm is pathological, and arthroscopy (not the squeeze test) is the gold standard diagnostic tool for probing syndesmotic diastasis.
items.note: Factually precise question testing key syndesmotic sprain concepts.

items.q: Primary ankle osteoarthritis is uncommon compared to hip and knee osteoarthritis. Which of the following correctly describes the biomechanical and biochemical properties of ankle articular cartilage?
o: Ankle cartilage is thicker than knee cartilage and exhibits a heightened catabolic response to interleukin-1 (IL-1).
Ankle cartilage has higher proteoglycan content, is stiffer, and has a smaller contact area with high congruency compared to knee cartilage.
Primary osteoarthritis accounts for 70–80% of all cases of end-stage ankle osteoarthritis.
Patients with end-stage ankle osteoarthritis report significantly less functional disability on SF-36 scores than those with end-stage hip osteoarthritis.
items.e: Ankle articular cartilage is thinner (1–1.7 mm) but more resistant to OA than knee cartilage due to higher proteoglycan content, higher stiffness, lower response to IL-1, and a smaller contact area with high congruency. Post-traumatic etiology (not primary OA) accounts for 70–80% of cases, and disability scores on SF-36 are comparable to end-stage hip OA.
items.note: Directly tested basic science concept in foot and ankle superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 42-year-old active manual worker presents with painful asymmetric varus ankle osteoarthritis. Weight-bearing radiographs show Takakura stage 3A arthritis with medial gutter obliteration but more than 50% preserved joint space laterally. Hindfoot alignment is flexible. Which of the following is the most appropriate joint-preserving surgical intervention and alignment goal for this patient?
o: Total ankle replacement using a 3-component mobile-bearing prosthesis
Medial closing-wedge tibial osteotomy targeting 5° of postoperative hindfoot varus
Medial opening-wedge distal tibial osteotomy overcorrecting to approximately 2-4° of valgus
Distraction arthroplasty with a 15 mm gap in a circular frame for 12 months
items.e: Supramalleolar osteotomy (SMOT) is indicated for asymmetric varus ankle OA with at least 50% preserved joint surface (Takakura 2–3A) in younger active patients. For varus OA, a medial opening-wedge (or lateral closing-wedge) tibial osteotomy is performed, overcorrecting slightly to 2–4° of valgus.
items.note: Clear clinical scenario testing indications and alignment targets of supramalleolar osteotomy.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient with severe end-stage ankle osteoarthritis is being evaluated for total ankle replacement (TAR). Which of the following conditions represents an absolute contraindication to total ankle replacement?
o: Mild inflammatory arthritis with a good soft-tissue envelope
Active or recent local joint infection
items.e: Active or recent infection is an absolute contraindication to total ankle replacement (along with Charcot neuroarthropathy, large talar AVN, severe peripheral arterial disease, and uncorrectable severe deformity or instability). Contralateral ankle fusion, older age, and inflammatory arthritis are established indications for TAR.
items.note: Standard contraindication question, clean and unambiguous.

items.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the deep component of the deltoid ligament complex of the ankle joint?
o: It consists of the tibiospring, tibionavicular, and tibiocalcaneal ligaments.
Its primary biomechanical function is to resist hindfoot eversion.
It includes the anterior and posterior tibiotalar ligaments and acts as the primary restraint to lateral talar shift.
A medial clear space of under 2 mm on an external rotation stress view confirms deep deltoid disruption.
items.e: The deep deltoid ligament consists of the anterior and posterior tibiotalar ligaments, which act as the primary restraint to lateral talar shift and external rotation. The superficial deltoid (tibiospring, tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal) resists hindfoot eversion. A medial clear space > 4-5 mm on stress views indicates deep deltoid insufficiency.
items.note: Anatomical and biomechanical core question, fully verified.

items.q: A 22-year-old basketball player lands awkwardly on an opponent's foot, sustaining an acute inversion injury in plantarflexion. On evaluation in the emergency department, he has acute pain over the lateral malleolus. According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, a plain radiographic series of the ankle is mandatory if which of the following criteria is met?
o: Inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately after the injury and in the emergency department
Any localized soft-tissue swelling around the lateral malleolus regardless of tenderness
Tenderness isolated over the calcaneofibular ligament on the floor of the peroneal sheath
Positive anterior drawer test measuring 2 mm side-to-side difference
items.e: Under the Ottawa Ankle Rules, ankle radiographs are indicated if there is pain in the malleolar zone AND bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm) OR an inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately after the injury and in the emergency department.
items.note: Classic evidence-based clinical decision rule question.

items.q: A 30-year-old male presents following a high-energy motor vehicle accident with a displaced talar neck fracture accompanied by dislocation of both the subtalar and tibiotalar (ankle) joints, while the talonavicular joint remains reduced. According to the Hawkins classification (modified by Canale and Kelly), how is this fracture classified and what is the estimated risk of avascular necrosis (AVN)?
items.e: Hawkins Type III talar neck fracture involves displacement with dislocation of both the subtalar and tibiotalar (ankle) joints. Due to extensive intraosseous and extraosseous soft tissue blood supply disruption, the risk of AVN is extremely high (50-100%).
items.note: Accurate, clear high-yield question completely aligned with standard text notes.

items.q: A lateral radiograph of the ankle and foot in a construction worker who fell from a ladder reveals a displaced intra-articular fracture of the calcaneus with depression of the posterior facet. Which of the following changes in radiographic angles is characteristically seen in this injury?
o: Increased Böhler angle and increased critical angle of Gissane
Reduced Böhler angle and increased critical angle of Gissane
Reduced Böhler angle and decreased critical angle of Gissane
Increased Böhler angle and decreased critical angle of Gissane
items.e: In depressed intra-articular calcaneal fractures, displacement of the posterior facet causes a reduction or collapse of the Böhler angle (normal 20-40 degrees) and an increase in the critical angle of Gissane (normal 95-105 degrees).
items.note: Standard high-yield anatomical/radiographic question.

items.q: A 24-year-old snowboarder presents with lateral ankle and hindfoot pain following a fall involving dorsiflexion, inversion, and axial load. Physical examination reveals focal tenderness just anterior and inferior to the tip of the lateral malleolus. Standard radiographs are inconclusive, and the injury is initially suspected to be a severe lateral ankle sprain. Which fracture is most likely present?
o: Shepherd fracture of the posterior process of the talus
Cedell fracture of the posterior process of the talus
Fracture of the lateral process of the talus
Avulsion fracture of the anterior process of the calcaneus
items.e: Fracture of the lateral process of the talus is famously known as 'snowboarder's fracture' (mechanism: dorsiflexion + inversion/eversion with axial load). It presents with point tenderness anterior and inferior to the tip of the lateral malleolus and is commonly misdiagnosed as an ankle sprain; CT is essential for confirmation.
items.note: Classic sub-speciality exam question, fully accurate.

items.q: A 38-year-old male presents with a closed Essex-Lopresti tongue-type calcaneal fracture. Clinical examination demonstrates significant displacement of the tuberosity fragment causing severe blanching and tenting of the posterior heel skin. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Application of a non-weight-bearing cast and delay of intervention for 7-14 days until the wrinkle sign appears
Urgent reduction and percutaneous fixation within 24 hours to relieve skin tension
Immediate extensile lateral open reduction and internal fixation through swollen soft tissues
items.e: Tongue-type calcaneal fractures with posterior skin tenting represent a soft-tissue emergency because the sharp bony fragment can rapidly lead to posterior skin necrosis. Urgent reduction (e.g., Essex-Lopresti manoeuvre and percutaneous pin/screw fixation) within 24 hours is required to relieve skin tension.
items.note: High-yield surgical emergency question, fully supported by reference notes.

items.q: A 28-year-old patient presents with a lateral subtalar (peritalar) dislocation following high-energy trauma. Closed reduction under sedation fails. Which anatomic structure is most commonly interposed, blocking closed reduction in a lateral subtalar dislocation?
items.e: In lateral subtalar dislocations, the tibialis posterior tendon is the most common mechanical block to closed reduction due to tendon interposition. In medial subtalar dislocations, the commonest block is buttonholing of the talar head through the extensor digitorum brevis or extensor retinaculum.
items.note: Classic board question, highly accurate.

items.q: Which dedicated radiographic projection is specifically performed with the foot in 15 degrees of pronation and the X-ray beam angled 75 degrees cephalad to best evaluate the talar neck for alignment, displacement, and shortening?
items.e: The Canale view (15-degree pronated foot, 75-degree cephalad-tilted AP of the foot) is the classic radiographic projection designed to obtain an true AP profile of the talar neck without superimposition of the calcaneus.
items.note: Direct, standard technical radiographic question.

items.q: A 52-year-old male who suffered a calcaneal fracture 4 years ago presents with severe chronic subtalar joint pain, marked loss of hindfoot height, a horizontal talus, and symptomatic anterior ankle impingement. Which operative procedure is specifically indicated to treat the subtalar arthritis while simultaneously restoring talar declination and calcaneal height?
items.e: Subtalar bone-block distraction arthrodesis is indicated for late post-traumatic subtalar arthritis accompanied by significant loss of calcaneal height, as it uses a bone graft to restore calcaneal height, correct talar declination (preventing anterior ankle impingement), and fuse the subtalar joint.
items.note: Classic post-traumatic reconstruction decision question.

items.q: Coronal CT images through the widest part of the posterior facet of the calcaneus demonstrate a four-part highly comminuted posterior facet fracture. According to the Sanders CT classification, how is this fracture classified and what is the generally recommended operative management in suitable surgical candidates?
o: Sanders Type III; sinus tarsi approach and screw fixation
Sanders Type IV; primary subtalar arthrodesis
Sanders Type IV; calcaneal tuberosity avulsion repair
items.e: Sanders Type IV calcaneal fractures involve four or more articular fragments with severe comminution of the posterior facet on coronal CT scans. Because functional outcomes following standard ORIF are historically poor, primary subtalar arthrodesis (combined with restoration of calcaneal body shape) is often recommended.
items.note: Standard classification and treatment indication question.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of a painful, non-structural scoliosis and muscle spasm. Radiographs reveal a small radiolucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis located in the lumbar spine posterior elements. Where is the lesion expected to be located relative to the scoliotic curve?
o: Concave side at the apex of the curve
Convex side at the apex of the curve
Concave side at the superior neutral vertebra
Convex side at the inferior neutral vertebra
items.e: In painful scoliosis caused by an osteoid osteoma of the spine, the lesion (nidus) is characteristically located on the concave side at the apex of the scoliotic curve due to localized paravertebral muscle spasm.
items.note: Accurate, standard SS question with precise spatial relation tested.

items.q: According to the Mankin principles for biopsy of a suspected primary malignant bone tumour, which of the following represents correct technical execution?
o: The biopsy tract should traverse intermuscular planes to avoid muscle belly contamination
Transarticular biopsy approaches are preferred for distal femoral metaphyseal lesions
The biopsy tract must be placed directly in line with the planned definitive surgical incision
Biopsy drains should be brought out distant from the planned resection incision to protect the skin
items.e: Mankin biopsy rules dictate that the core needle or open biopsy tract must lie directly in line with the planned definitive incision so that it can be excised en bloc during definitive limb-salvage surgery. The tract must pass through a single muscle compartment and avoid intermuscular planes, joints, and neurovascular bundles.
items.note: Exemplary question on biopsy principles in musculoskeletal oncology.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a hard mass on the posterior aspect of her distal femur. Plain radiography demonstrates a broad-based dense lobulated bone mass with a radiolucent cleavage line ('string sign') separating it from the cortex. Which histological pattern distinguishes parosteal osteosarcoma from myositis ossificans?
o: Densest mature bone centrally at the base with less mature bone at the periphery
Peripheral mature lamellar bone surrounding an immature central osteoid core
Diffuse geographic lucency with ground-glass matrix and woven trabeculae
Small round blue cells producing thin intercellular osteoid
items.e: Parosteal osteosarcoma displays a 'reverse zonal pattern' where the lesion is densest and most mature centrally at its base near the bone cortex, becoming less mature at the periphery. In contrast, myositis ossificans shows a zonal pattern with peripheral maturation into mature lamellar bone surrounding an immature central core.
items.note: Classic diagnostic differentiator, perfectly accurate.

items.q: Following neoadjuvant MAP chemotherapy for a high-grade conventional osteosarcoma of the distal femur, the resected specimen undergoes histological evaluation of tumour necrosis. According to the Rosen-Huvos grading system, what is the minimum threshold of tumour necrosis required to classify the patient as a 'good responder'?
items.e: Under the Rosen-Huvos grading system, a good histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy is defined as 90% or greater tumour necrosis (Huvos Grade III: 90-99%, Grade IV: 100% necrosis). Patients with less than 90% necrosis are classified as poor responders (Grade I or II).
items.note: High-yield prognostic standard in osteosarcoma.

items.q: An 18-year-old male presents with a painful, expansile, purely lytic lesion of the distal femoral metaphysis. MRI demonstrates multiple fluid-fluid levels within the lesion. Which feature on dynamic contrast MRI or histology strongly points to telangiectatic osteosarcoma rather than a primary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC)?
o: Thin, smooth peripheral rim enhancement with thin fibrous septa
Thick, nodular enhancing septa containing pleomorphic malignant cells
Presence of GNAS gene mutation within benign stromal cells
Absence of soft tissue extension or cortical erosion
items.e: While both telangiectatic osteosarcoma and aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) show fluid-fluid levels on MRI, telangiectatic osteosarcoma features thick, nodular enhancing septa containing pleomorphic malignant cells producing osteoid, whereas ABC has thin, benign fibrous septa.
items.note: Crucial radiological-pathological differential diagnosis.

items.q: Osteomas of the skull and facial bones can be a presenting feature of Gardner syndrome. Which of the following clinical features or genetic alterations is characteristic of this syndrome?
o: Familial adenomatous polyposis due to APC gene mutation on chromosome 5q
items.e: Gardner syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by multiple osteomas, familial adenomatous polyposis (APC gene mutation on chromosome 5q), desmoid tumours, and epidermoid cysts. Colonic polyps have near 100% malignant potential, making detection of jaw osteomas a critical clue.
items.note: Standard syndromic oncology question.

items.q: The EURAMOS-1 trial evaluated treatment strategies in conventional osteosarcoma based on histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. What was the main finding regarding post-operative chemotherapy in poor responders (<90% necrosis)?
o: Adding ifosfamide and etoposide (MAPIE) significantly improved event-free survival
Intensifying post-operative chemotherapy (MAPIE) failed to improve event-free survival and increased toxicity
Switching to adjuvant proton-beam radiotherapy significantly improved local control
Adding pegylated interferon alfa-2b doubled overall 5-year survival
items.e: The EURAMOS-1 trial demonstrated that intensifying post-operative chemotherapy by adding ifosfamide and etoposide (MAPIE) to MAP in poor responders did not improve event-free survival and increased toxicity. MAP remains the standard regimen regardless of necrosis percentage.
items.note: Landmark trial question tested frequently in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 7-year-old child undergoes a Van Nes rotationplasty following wide resection of a distal femoral conventional osteosarcoma. In this procedure, how is the distal limb rotated, and which ankle motion corresponds to knee extension?
o: Rotated 90 degrees; ankle dorsiflexion acts as knee extension
Rotated 180 degrees; ankle dorsiflexion acts as knee extension
Rotated 270 degrees; ankle inversion acts as knee extension
Rotated 180 degrees; ankle plantarflexion acts as knee extension
items.e: In Van Nes rotationplasty, the distal leg is rotated 180 degrees and attached to the femur so that the ankle joint functions as a knee joint. Ankle plantarflexion drives knee extension, allowing the patient to actively control a below-knee type prosthesis.
items.note: Surgical anatomy and biomechanics correctly captured.

items.q: A 16-year-old male presents with persistent shoulder pain and a joint effusion. Radiographs reveal a well-defined lytic lesion in the proximal humeral epiphysis with a thin sclerotic rim. MRI shows extensive surrounding bone marrow oedema. Which of the following molecular markers is most specific for confirming the diagnosis?
items.e: The clinical and radiological description fits Chondroblastoma (Codman tumour), which characteristically occurs in the epiphysis of skeletally immature patients and shows disproportionate oedema on MRI. The H3F3B K36M (H3.3) mutation is a highly specific molecular marker for this tumour.
items.note: The question accurately tests the clinical, radiological, and molecular hallmarks of chondroblastoma as per the provided notes.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman with a history of solitary osteochondroma of the proximal tibia reports new-onset pain and increasing swelling at the site. Which MRI finding is the most reliable indicator of malignant transformation to a secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma?
o: Fracture of the stalk of the lesion
Presence of an overlying adventitial bursa
Corticomedullary continuity with the host bone
items.e: In an adult, a cartilage cap thicker than 2 cm is a major warning sign of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. Stalk fractures and bursitis are common causes of pain in benign osteochondromas, while corticomedullary continuity is a defining feature of the benign lesion itself.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the threshold for malignancy in the cartilage cap of an osteochondroma, distinguishing it from benign causes of pain.

items.q: According to the Masada classification of forearm deformities in Hereditary Multiple Exostoses (HME), which type is defined by radial head dislocation secondary to a short ulna caused by a distal ulnar lesion, without a proximal radial lesion?
items.e: Masada Type IIb involves radial head dislocation secondary to ulnar shortening from a distal ulnar osteochondroma, without a lesion in the proximal radius. Type IIa involves a proximal radial lesion, while Type I has no radial head dislocation.
items.note: The question accurately tests the specific subtypes of the Masada classification, which is a standard exam topic for HME.

items.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painful lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the proximal femur. Histological examination shows clear cells interspersed with osteoclast-like giant cells. What is the most appropriate management for this lesion?
o: Observation with serial MRI every 6 months
items.e: The diagnosis is Clear Cell Chondrosarcoma, which is a low-grade malignant tumour that typically occurs in the epiphysis of adults (mimicking chondroblastoma). Unlike its benign look-alikes, it requires wide en bloc resection because curettage results in high recurrence rates.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the management of a specific chondrosarcoma subtype based on its clinical and histological presentation.

items.q: Which radiographic feature is most useful in distinguishing an atypical cartilaginous tumour (ACT) / Grade 1 chondrosarcoma of the femur from a benign enchondroma?
o: Location in the medullary cavity of the metaphysis
Endosteal scalloping involving more than two-thirds of the cortical thickness
items.e: Deep endosteal scalloping (greater than two-thirds of the cortical thickness) and a length of scalloping over two-thirds of the lesion are key indicators of ACT/Chondrosarcoma. Enchondromas typically show little to no scalloping.
items.note: The question tests the critical radiographic criteria used to differentiate benign from locally aggressive cartilage lesions in long bones.

items.q: A 22-year-old presents with an eccentric, lobulated lytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis. Radiographs show a prominent sclerotic, 'bite-like' scalloped margin, but no internal calcification. Histology reveals stellate cells in a myxoid stroma with hypercellular lobular peripheries. What is the likely diagnosis?
items.e: Chondromyxoid fibroma (CMF) is a rare benign tumour that typically presents as an eccentric, metaphyseal lesion in the proximal tibia with a scalloped sclerotic rim. Unlike most other cartilage tumours, internal calcification is uncommon on radiographs.
items.note: The question accurately combines the classic site, radiographic appearance, and histology of CMF.

items.q: A 19-year-old is diagnosed with a mesenchymal chondrosarcoma of the ribs. Which of the following statements regarding this tumour is correct?
o: It is characterized by the HEY1-NCOA2 fusion gene
It is typically treated with surgery alone as it is radiotherapy resistant
The histology shows pure hyaline cartilage with high mitotic activity
It is most common in patients over the age of 60
items.e: Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is characterized by the HEY1-NCOA2 fusion. It is a biphasic tumour (small round blue cells and hyaline cartilage islands) that occurs in younger patients and, unlike conventional chondrosarcoma, is sensitive to Ewing-type chemotherapy regimens.
items.note: The question tests high-yield molecular and clinical facts about a specific malignant subtype.

items.q: A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with a Grade 2 conventional chondrosarcoma of the ilium. What is the primary treatment of choice?
o: Extended intralesional curettage with liquid nitrogen adjuvant
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by marginal resection
items.e: Conventional chondrosarcomas are resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy. For axial Grade 1 lesions and all Grade 2 or 3 lesions, wide en bloc resection is the mainstay of treatment. Intralesional curettage is only considered for ACT/Grade 1 lesions in the appendicular skeleton.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the surgical management of high-grade axial chondrosarcoma based on its known resistance to adjuvant therapies.

items.q: A 34-year-old female presents with a lytic lesion in the distal femoral epiphysis extending to the subchondral bone. Radiographs show a geographic lesion with a well-defined margin but no sclerotic rim. According to the Lodwick classification, this pattern of growth is categorized as:
items.e: Lodwick Grade IB refers to a geographic, well-defined lytic lesion without a sclerotic rim, typical of active lesions like giant cell tumour (GCT) or myeloma. Grade IA has a sclerotic rim, indicating a slower growth rate.
items.note: The question correctly applies the Lodwick classification to the clinical presentation of a GCT as described in the reference notes.

items.q: In the pathogenesis of Giant Cell Tumour of Bone (GCTB), which cell population is the true neoplastic component and what is its most characteristic molecular marker?
o: Mononuclear stromal cells; H3F3A (H3.3) G34W mutation
Osteoclast-like giant cells; H3F3A (H3.3) G34W mutation
items.e: The mononuclear stromal cells are the neoplastic cells in GCTB and express RANKL. Over 90% carry the H3F3A G34W mutation. The giant cells are reactive, recruited osteoclasts that express RANK.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the current molecular understanding of GCTB as detailed in the provided notes.

items.q: An 8-year-old boy is diagnosed with a large Unicameral Bone Cyst (UBC) in the proximal femur. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy to prevent complications like varus malunion or avascular necrosis?
o: Curettage, bone grafting, and internal fixation
Wide en bloc resection and reconstruction
items.e: Proximal femoral UBCs carry a high risk of pathological fracture, varus malunion, and growth arrest. The source notes recommend surgical treatment with curettage, grafting, and internal fixation (e.g., pediatric hip screw or nails) for these high-risk sites.
items.note: The management strategy for high-risk UBC sites like the proximal femur is correctly identified based on the reference notes.

items.q: A 15-year-old presents with a blood-filled, multiloculated, expansile 'blow-out' lesion in the metaphysis of the humerus. Molecular analysis confirms a USP6 gene rearrangement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Primary ABC is a true neoplasm characterized by USP6 gene rearrangements (commonly CD11-USP6). Secondary ABCs occur within other tumours and lack this specific genetic rearrangement.
items.note: The question tests the specific molecular hallmark of primary ABC as stated in the notes.

items.q: Regarding the use of neoadjuvant Denosumab in a patient with a Giant Cell Tumour of the distal femur that is already amenable to joint-preserving curettage, which of the following is a significant clinical concern?
o: It causes malignant transformation in over 50% of cases
It increases the risk of intraoperative haemorrhage
It results in higher local recurrence rates after curettage
It makes the tumour more aggressive and increases lung implants
items.e: Denosumab induces thick new bone formation and a sclerotic rim that can hide residual neoplastic stromal cells. This makes thorough curettage difficult and is associated with higher local recurrence rates; thus, it is not routinely recommended before curettage.
items.note: This is a critical clinical pearl regarding the limitations of Denosumab in GCT management mentioned in the notes.

items.q: A 12-year-old girl with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and irregular 'coast of Maine' café-au-lait spots is being evaluated. Which metabolic association is part of the McCune-Albright syndrome spectrum in this patient?
items.e: McCune-Albright syndrome includes polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, and endocrinopathies such as precocious puberty and FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting leading to hypophosphataemic rickets.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the metabolic component of McCune-Albright syndrome as described in the notes.

items.q: Biopsy of a multiloculated lytic lesion in the anterior tibial cortex of a 6-year-old child shows woven bone trabeculae with prominent osteoblastic rimming in a fibrous stroma. No keratin-positive epithelial nests are identified. This description is most consistent with:
items.e: Osteofibrous dysplasia (Campanacci lesion) typically occurs in the anterior tibial cortex in children under 10 and is distinguished from fibrous dysplasia by the presence of osteoblastic rimming. The absence of keratin-positive epithelial nests distinguishes it from adamantinoma.
items.note: The histological and clinical distinctions between OFD, FD, and adamantinoma are accurately tested.

items.q: A 7-year-old child presents with a 'punched-out' skull lesion and a collapsed thoracic vertebra (vertebra plana). Biopsy of the skull lesion shows cells with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy. Which of the following markers will be positive on immunohistochemistry?
items.e: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is characterized by Langerhans cells that are positive for CD1a, CD207 (langerin), and S100. Birbeck granules ('tennis racquets') are the classic electron microscopy finding.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the pathognomonic markers and findings for LCH as per the reference notes.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a 10-cm tender mass involving the ilium. Biopsy reveals sheets of small round blue cells that are CD99 and NKX2.2 positive. Staging workup reveals multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Which of the following is the most important adverse prognostic factor for this patient?
o: The pelvic location of the primary tumour
The presence of distant metastases at diagnosis
The specific EWSR1-FLI1 fusion transcript type
items.e: According to the provided notes, the presence of metastases at diagnosis is the most important adverse prognostic factor in Ewing sarcoma. While pelvic site, large tumour volume (>200 mL), and older age are also unfavourable, they are secondary to the presence of distant disease.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the hierarchy of prognostic factors in Ewing sarcoma as per the provided notes and standard oncology literature.

items.q: Based on the results of the Euro Ewing 2012 trial (Brennan et al., 2022), which chemotherapy strategy is now established as the international standard of care for both North American and European protocols for Ewing sarcoma?
o: VIDE (vincristine, ifosfamide, doxorubicin, etoposide) induction for all patients
High-dose busulfan-melphalan with autologous stem-cell rescue for isolated pulmonary metastases
Interval-compressed VDC/IE (vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide, etoposide)
VDC/IE administered every 3 weeks to minimize haematological toxicity
items.e: The Euro Ewing 2012 trial demonstrated that interval-compressed VDC/IE (given every 2 weeks) was superior to the VIDE induction regimen in terms of event-free and overall survival with less toxicity, making it the current standard of care.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the landmark trial results mentioned in the reference notes which changed the standard of care.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of deep thigh pain. MRI shows a large circumferential soft-tissue mass surrounding the femoral diaphysis with extensive marrow replacement, but the underlying cortex appears remarkably intact. Biopsy reveals CD20 and CD45 positive small round cells. What is the most appropriate definitive management for the primary lesion?
o: Wide local resection and endoprosthetic reconstruction
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by limb-salvage surgery
Radical radiotherapy (60-65 Gy) as the sole treatment modality
items.e: The clinical picture (adult, large mass, intact cortex, CD20/CD45 positive) describes primary lymphoma of bone (DLBCL). The notes state that surgery has no role in tumour removal for this condition; management consists of chemotherapy (R-CHOP) with or without consolidation radiotherapy.
items.note: The question tests the recognition of primary bone lymphoma and its distinct non-surgical management compared to other bone tumours.

items.q: A 62-year-old male presents with sudden onset back pain. Imaging reveals a solitary, purely lytic lesion of the L3 vertebral body without a sclerotic rim. Which of the following findings would be a 'myeloma-defining event' according to the IMWG 2014 criteria, even in the absence of CRAB features?
o: Clonal bone marrow plasma cells of 40%
A single focal lesion of 4 mm on MRI
items.e: The IMWG 2014 SLiM biomarkers for myeloma include: Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60%, involved:uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio ≥100, and more than one focal lesion (≥5 mm) on MRI. A ratio of 110 qualifies as a myeloma-defining event.
items.note: The question correctly tests the specific SLiM-CRAB diagnostic criteria for multiple myeloma.

items.q: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with periorbital ecchymosis, proptosis, and a palpable abdominal mass. Radiographs show symmetric, permeative lytic lesions in the metaphyses of both proximal humeri. Which of the following is the most likely histological finding in the bone lesions?
o: Small cells with scant glycogen-rich cytoplasm and t(11;22)
Small cells with dot-like desmin and keratin positivity
Large B cells with CD20 positivity
items.e: The clinical presentation (under 5 years, raccoon eyes, abdominal mass, symmetric metaphyseal lesions) is classic for metastatic neuroblastoma. Histologically, neuroblastoma is characterized by small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes and neuropil.
items.note: The question tests the classic clinical and histological presentation of neuroblastoma in a paediatric orthopaedic context.

items.q: Regarding the 2020 WHO classification of small round cell tumours, which of the following 'Ewing-like' sarcomas is typically found in soft tissues and behaves more aggressively than classic Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: The WHO 2020 classification separates 'Ewing-like' sarcomas. CIC-rearranged (CIC-DUX4) sarcomas are mostly soft-tissue tumours and are noted in the source material to behave more aggressively than true Ewing sarcoma.
items.note: The question tests updated WHO classification terminology and clinical behavior as noted in the reference text.

items.q: A 16-year-old female is diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma of the distal femur. After 12 weeks of induction chemotherapy, she undergoes wide resection. Histological analysis shows 15% viable tumour cells in the resection specimen. Based on this finding, what is the next step in management according to standard protocols?
o: Observation and completion of chemotherapy only
Postoperative radiotherapy to the tumour bed
Immediate amputation to ensure local control
Changing chemotherapy to an osteosarcoma-based protocol
items.e: A poor histological response in Ewing sarcoma is defined as 10% or more viable cells. The notes state that surgery plus postoperative radiotherapy is indicated for poor histological response or inadequate margins.
items.note: The question tests the threshold for 'poor response' and the subsequent management change in Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding the orthopaedic management of multiple myeloma is correct?
o: Bone scintigraphy is the investigation of choice to screen for impending fractures
Pathological fractures in myeloma have the highest healing rate among bone metastatic lesions
Internal fixation should be limited to the lesion site to avoid bone marrow contamination
Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is a reliable indicator of bone destruction
items.e: As per the notes, pathological fractures in myeloma have the highest healing rate (about two-thirds heal). Bone scans are often falsely negative due to lack of osteoblastic activity, ALP is usually normal, and intramedullary nails should protect the whole bone.
items.note: The question tests key clinical pearls regarding myeloma bone disease, including healing rates and the limitations of standard imaging like bone scans.

items.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painless, 8 cm deep-seated mass in the thigh that has been slowly enlarging for 6 months. Which is the most appropriate next step in management according to the principles established by Mankin et al.?
o: Immediate excisional biopsy at the local hospital
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) to confirm the diagnosis
Contrast-enhanced MRI followed by core needle biopsy at a specialist sarcoma centre
Incisional biopsy using a transverse incision to maximize exposure
items.e: Mankin demonstrated that biopsies performed at referring hospitals have significantly higher rates of diagnostic errors and complications. Management should follow imaging (MRI) and be performed at the specialist centre using a longitudinal core needle biopsy.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the Mankin principles and the standard diagnostic pathway for soft-tissue sarcomas.

items.q: Lymph node metastasis is uncommon in soft-tissue sarcomas, occurring in less than 5% of cases. Which of the following histological subtypes is most likely to exhibit regional lymph node spread?
items.e: While rare overall, lymph node spread is characteristic of the 'SCARE' group: Synovial sarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, and Epithelioid sarcoma.
items.note: The 'SCARE' mnemonic is a classic exam fact for lymph-node-seeking sarcomas.

items.q: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with a high-grade myxoid liposarcoma of the thigh. In addition to a CT of the chest, which staging investigation is specifically indicated due to the unique metastatic pattern of this subtype?
items.e: Myxoid liposarcoma is known for metastasizing to extrapulmonary sites like the spine, retroperitoneum, and other soft tissues, which may be missed on standard CT chest or PET scans. Whole-spine or whole-body MRI is recommended.
items.note: This tests a specific, high-yield staging requirement for myxoid liposarcoma mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: According to the NCIC SR2 trial (O'Sullivan et al.), what is the primary clinical trade-off when choosing preoperative radiotherapy over postoperative radiotherapy for an extremity soft-tissue sarcoma?
o: Preoperative radiotherapy has better local control but higher risk of metastasis
Preoperative radiotherapy has higher wound complications but lower late toxicity (fibrosis/stiffness)
Postoperative radiotherapy has fewer wound complications but a significantly higher risk of amputation
Preoperative radiotherapy is associated with higher overall survival
items.e: The O'Sullivan trial showed that preoperative radiotherapy (50 Gy) results in a 35% wound complication rate compared to 17% for postoperative radiotherapy, but preoperative treatment results in less permanent late toxicity like fibrosis and joint stiffness.
items.note: This is a fundamental trial in orthopaedic oncology that dictates current treatment protocols.

items.q: A 65-year-old female has a large, deep-seated lipomatous mass in her thigh. FISH analysis reveals MDM2 and CDK4 amplification on ring chromosomes. What is the most appropriate surgical strategy for this lesion?
o: Wide excision with 2 cm margins and adjuvant radiotherapy
Marginal excision, as this tumor does not metastasize in the extremities
Radical compartmental resection to prevent dedifferentiation
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by wide excision
items.e: Atypical lipomatous tumours (ALT/Well-differentiated liposarcoma) are characterized by MDM2 amplification. In the extremities, they do not metastasize, and marginal excision is considered acceptable management.
items.note: The question tests the specific biological behavior and management of ALT/WDL as per the reference notes.

items.q: A 22-year-old presents with a painful, slow-growing mass in the popliteal fossa. Radiographs show speckled calcifications within the soft tissue mass. Which molecular finding would confirm the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Synovial sarcoma typically affects young adults around the knee and exhibits calcification in 30% of cases. It is characterized by the t(X;18) translocation involving the SS18 and SSX genes.
items.note: Tests the classic presentation and genetics of synovial sarcoma.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with an asymptomatic, 4 cm desmoid-type fibromatosis of the shoulder girdle. According to the 2020 Global Consensus, what is the preferred first-line management?
items.e: The 2020 Global Consensus recommends active surveillance as the first-line management for most desmoid tumours, as many stabilize or regress spontaneously. Surgery or systemic therapy is reserved for progressive or symptomatic disease.
items.note: Reflects the major shift in desmoid management mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: The FNCLCC (French) grading system, which is the standard for histological grading of soft-tissue sarcomas, is based on which three parameters?
o: Tumor size, depth, and mitotic count
Tumor differentiation, mitotic count, and tumor necrosis
Tumor size, necrosis, and lymph node status
Tumor differentiation, vascular invasion, and depth
items.e: The FNCLCC grading system uses three parameters: tumor differentiation (1-3), mitotic count (1-3), and tumor necrosis (0-2). Tumor size and depth are staging parameters, not grading parameters.
items.note: Tests the specific components of the most widely used histological grading system for STS.

items.q: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with a painful, destructive lesion of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Radiographs show a purely lytic lesion with no matrix calcification. What is the most likely primary site for this lesion?
items.e: Acrometastases (lesions distal to the elbow and knee) are rare. When they occur, the most common primary site is the lung.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the lung as the most common primary for acrometastases as per the reference notes.

items.q: A 55-year-old female with breast cancer has a 2.5 cm lytic lesion in the peritrochanteric region of the femur. She reports significant mechanical pain on weight-bearing. Radiographically, the lesion involves half of the bone diameter. What is her calculated Mirels score?
items.e: Mirels score: Site (Peritrochanteric = 3), Pain (Functional/Mechanical = 3), Lesion (Lytic = 3), Size (1/3 to 2/3 = 2). Total = 11. A score of 9 or more indicates prophylactic fixation.
items.note: The calculation is accurate based on the Mirels scoring system provided in the reference notes.

items.q: In differentiating a malignant vertebral collapse from an osteoporotic insufficiency fracture on MRI, which of the following features is most suggestive of a malignant etiology?
o: Band-like edema with preserved fatty marrow
Convex bulge of the posterior cortex
items.e: Malignant vertebral collapse typically shows a convex bulge of the posterior cortex, diffuse T1 low signal replacing the whole body, and involvement of the pedicles. The fluid sign and vacuum cleft are characteristic of osteoporotic fractures.
items.note: The features listed correctly distinguish between malignant and osteoporotic collapse according to the MRI criteria in the notes.

items.q: A 62-year-old man presents with a solitary, expansile 'blow-out' lytic lesion in the proximal humerus. Biopsy confirms metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Which preoperative intervention is most critical to perform 24-72 hours before definitive surgical fixation?
items.e: Renal cell and thyroid metastases are highly vascular (often presenting as expansile 'blow-out' lesions). Preoperative embolization is essential to reduce massive intraoperative blood loss.
items.note: The question tests a critical surgical principle for hypervascular metastases (renal/thyroid) mentioned in the notes.

items.q: The landmark randomized trial by Patchell et al. (2005) demonstrated that for patients with metastatic spinal cord compression from solid tumors:
o: Radiotherapy alone is superior to surgery for maintaining walking
Direct decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy is superior to radiotherapy alone for maintaining ambulation
Laminectomy alone is the surgical procedure of choice
Surgery is only beneficial if the patient has been paraplegic for more than 48 hours
items.e: The Patchell study showed that circumferential decompression and stabilization followed by radiotherapy was significantly better than radiotherapy alone for maintaining and regaining ambulation in patients with solid tumor MSCC.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the findings and inclusion criteria of the landmark Patchell trial cited in the notes.

items.q: A patient with a periacetabular metastasis is found to have a deficient medial wall, while the lateral cortex and superior dome (roof) remain intact. According to the Harrington classification, this is categorized as:
items.e: Harrington Class II involves a deficient medial wall. Class I has intact walls/roof, Class III has a deficient lateral cortex or superior roof, and Class IV is a solitary lesion treated for cure.
items.note: The classification matches the Harrington criteria for periacetabular defects provided in the reference.

items.q: In the 'vicious cycle' of osteolytic bone metastasis, tumor cells secrete factors like PTHrP that primarily stimulate which of the following steps?
o: Direct tumor-cell resorption of bone matrix
Inhibition of TGF-beta release from the matrix
items.e: Tumor cells secrete PTHrP, which stimulates osteoblasts to increase RANKL expression. RANKL then activates osteoclasts to resorb bone, which in turn releases growth factors like TGF-beta that further stimulate the tumor.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the molecular mechanism of the osteolytic vicious cycle as described in the pathophysiology section.

items.q: Which of the following is the preferred surgical treatment for a metastatic lesion of the femoral neck in an elderly patient with an estimated survival of 6 months?
o: Cemented hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty
items.e: Metastatic lesions of the femoral head and neck do not heal reliably. Therefore, replacement (cemented hemiarthroplasty or THA) is preferred over internal fixation to allow immediate weight-bearing and ensure the construct outlasts the patient.
items.note: The question follows the surgical principle that femoral neck metastases should be replaced rather than fixed, as stated in the reference notes.

items.q: A 19-year-old male presents with a suspected primary osteosarcoma of the proximal humerus. Which of the following is the most appropriate biopsy route to minimize compartment contamination and facilitate later limb-salvage surgery?
items.e: According to standard biopsy principles, the proximal humerus should be biopsied through the anterior third of the deltoid. The deltopectoral groove must be avoided because it would contaminate the pectoralis major, cephalic vein, and the deltopectoral plane, complicating future resection.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the preferred biopsy route for the proximal humerus as per Campbell's and the provided notes.

items.q: According to the Enneking (MSTS) staging for malignant bone tumours, a high-grade tumour that has breached the cortex into the soft tissues but has no evidence of regional or distant metastasis is classified as:
items.e: Enneking Stage IIB represents a high-grade (G2), extracompartmental (T2) lesion without metastasis (M0). A bone tumour becomes extracompartmental once it breaches the natural barrier of the cortex. This is the most common stage at presentation for osteosarcoma.
items.note: The staging criteria for Enneking IIB are accurately applied based on the grade and compartmental status.

items.q: A 62-year-old male with a destructive lytic lesion of the humerus is undergoing systemic staging. Which of the following conditions is most likely to result in a 'cold' (false-negative) result on a Tc-99m MDP bone scan?
items.e: Myeloma typically presents as purely lytic lesions with no osteoblastic response, often leading to a false-negative (cold) bone scan. For these patients, a skeletal survey, whole-body MRI, or PET-CT is preferred for staging.
items.note: The fact that myeloma is often cold on bone scans is a classic exam fact supported by the notes.

items.q: In the surgical technique of an open incisional biopsy for a suspected extremity sarcoma, which of the following is a recommended rule to prevent treatment complications?
o: Use a transverse incision to allow for wider skin flaps
Dissect through the internervous plane to identify neurovascular bundles
Exsanguinate the limb with an Esmarch bandage before tourniquet inflation
Place the surgical drain in line with and close to the incision
items.e: Drains must be placed in line with and close to the incision so the entire tract can be excised en bloc. Transverse incisions, intermuscular/internervous dissections, and Esmarch exsanguination are avoided as they increase the risk of tumour spread or contamination of multiple compartments.
items.note: The technical rules for biopsy are correctly represented, specifically the placement of the drain.

items.q: Under the AJCC 8th edition staging system for primary bone tumours, which of the following findings would specifically categorize a patient as Stage IVB?
o: Presence of skip lesions in the same bone
items.e: In the AJCC 8th edition for bone tumours, Stage IVA is defined by lung-only metastasis (M1a). Stage IVB is defined by regional lymph node metastasis (N1) or other distant metastases such as to other bones (M1b).
items.note: The distinction between Stage IVA and IVB in the AJCC 8th edition for bone is a high-yield exam point correctly tested here.

items.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a diaphyseal bone lesion. Radiographs show a purely 'permeative' pattern of bone destruction with no identifiable geographic margins. According to the Lodwick-Madewell grading system, this is classified as:
items.e: Lodwick-Madewell Grade III is characterized by a purely moth-eaten or permeative pattern without geographic margins, indicating a fast-growing, aggressive lesion such as Ewing sarcoma, lymphoma, or osteomyelitis.
items.note: The Lodwick-Madewell classification for aggressive bone destruction is correctly applied.

items.q: What is the primary rationale for performing local staging with MRI before obtaining a biopsy in a patient with a suspected bone sarcoma?
o: To obtain a definitive histological diagnosis
Biopsy-induced haematoma and oedema can distort MRI and overstate tumour extent
MRI is required to guide the specific molecular translocation testing
To determine the Huvos grade of the tumour before surgery
items.e: MRI must be done before biopsy because the resulting haematoma and inflammatory oedema from the biopsy can distort the anatomical planes on MRI, leading to an overestimation of the tumour's local extent and marrow involvement.
items.note: The sequence of staging is a fundamental principle in orthopaedic oncology.

items.q: A biopsy is performed on a suspected aggressive bone tumour. Molecular analysis reveals a characteristic H3F3A (H3.3) G34W mutation. This finding is highly specific for which of the following?
items.e: The H3F3A G34W mutation is a characteristic molecular marker for Giant Cell Tumour (GCT) of bone. In contrast, Chondroblastoma is associated with the H3F3B K36M mutation.
